facts.text: Carmel Valley Village sits on land once granted as Rancho Los Laureles, a 6,625‑acre Mexican estate awarded in 1839 by Governor Alvarado.
After World War II, the community expanded and adopted the name Carmel Valley Village, shifting its identity from an aviation hub to a residential enclave.
From the 1960s through the 1990s, the Jamesburg Earth Station in Carmel Valley transmitted Intelsat’s global communications network, even relaying Apollo 11’s first‑step video.
Indigenous peoples, including the Rumsen Ohlone and possibly the Esselen, have inhabited the lower Carmel River valley for at least 2,000 years.
In 1882, the Pacific Improvement Company bought Rancho Los Laureles to support regional development, diverting water for irrigation and expanding dairy production for Del Monte.
The Carmel River snakes northwest through the village, eventually emptying into the Pacific at Carmel‑by‑the‑Sea, shaping the local landscape.
